ledger.hypothesis: The node is not query-shaped and not elementwise-shaped -- it is a dense-factorisation shape. A is (M+4)x(M+4) = 1566x1566, and nd::inv runs Gauss-Jordan on an augmented n x 2n buffer, so the inner loop executes n*n*2n = 7.7e9 fused mul-sub. That is essentially 100% of the 2103 ms. Crucially inv(A) depends ONLY on restCage.points: rc, d2, K and the affine border of A are all functions of rest alone, while deformCage enters only through T and geoToDeform only through H. So the single most expensive object in the node is derived state of an input that is typically static while another input animates -- exactly the cache-the-factorisation case. Keying on an exact memcmp of the raw float point buffer (18 KB, ~5 us) rather than on a pointer/count heuristic makes a cache hit imply bit-identical inputs, hence a bit-identical cached value, so parity is safe by construction on both the GEO path (fresh upstream shape per config -> key differs -> rebuild) and the SCALAR path (geometry wired once -> key matches -> hit).
ledger.risk: Two real risks. (1) Staleness: a cache keyed on anything weaker than the full point data diverges when the GEO parity path re-wires a fresh shape, so the key is a byte-exact memcmp of the whole buffer, not a fingerprint that can collide. Invalidation is per-instance (RbfWrapState _state member, no static registry), mutex-guarded, and re-verified from setDependentsDirty and preEvaluation -- but those hooks only set pendingRecheck, they deliberately do NOT clear the cache, because dgdirty() marks every input dirty on every tick whether or not the data changed and clearing there would defeat the whole optimisation. (2) Reassociation: the tempting follow-on is W = solve(A,T) instead of inv(A)@T, or (H@invA)@T instead of H@(invA@T). Both are better-conditioned and cheaper and both change the last bits, so both were rejected -- the tolerance gate would pass them and byte parity would not. The matmul reschedule that WAS taken is safe for a documented reason rather than an assumed one: the runtime's own comment certifies i-l-j as bit-identical to i-j-l because each (i,j) still sums ascending l with one rounding per add, and the new kernel keeps the (A then B) operand order and never mixes the twelve accumulator chains.
ledger.theme: cache the three rest-cage-derived structures (inv(A), H, W) on the node instance behind an exact byte-compare of the raw point buffers, so a re-evaluation whose geometry did not actually change skips the 1566x1566 Gauss-Jordan inverse entirely; then read the 19.6 MB H operand once instead of three times in the final n==3 matmul.

ledger.hypothesis: the invA/H/W cross-evaluation cache from the previous round already removes the O(M^3) solve, so a cached tick is just H@W plus Maya mesh I/O; stage timers should show one dominant pass, and since row i of H@W is an ascending-l sum touching no other row, a disjoint row-range map over a persistent pool is bit-identical and should scale with cores until it hits DRAM bandwidth
ledger.risk: chunk boundaries must not change the answer -- they cannot here, because each row's three accumulators sum the same k terms in the same ascending order whether the row lands in the 4-row block or the scalar tail; the real risks are the pool (cursor must be a pool MEMBER so two concurrent EM instances cannot rewind each other, threads persistent and joined in ~RbfWrap, never per-evaluate) and the topology cache, which keys geoToDeform's counts/indices on the point-buffer byte fingerprint plus numPolygons/numFaceVertices rather than on the connectivity itself
ledger.theme: profile first, then thread the one pass that owns 75% of the tick -- the (Nn,M+4)@(M+4,3) evaluation matmul -- as a persistent-pool per-row map, and make everything the cache already covers lazy
